claims.text: Atomic-size mismatch among constituent elements produces local lattice distortion in solid-solution HEAs.
Local lattice distortion is the primary factor controlling superconducting critical temperature in superconducting HEAs.
Local lattice distortion controls Tc by modulating electron–phonon coupling strength.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase superconducting solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
Controlled chemical substitution with an element of a different atomic radius can systematically change average atomic-size mismatch and local lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatch can be varied by substitution without changing the overall valence-electron count or crystal structure.
XRD peak broadening or EXAFS can quantify the relevant local lattice distortion.
Local static strain fields alter interatomic distances.
Local static strain fields alter the phonon spectrum.
Lattice distortion changes the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Distortion-induced changes in phonons and electronic density of states modulate the electron–phonon coupling constant.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling alter the superconducting pairing interaction and Tc.
Increasing quantified lattice distortion will produce a measurable shift in Tc relative to the baseline alloy.
The direction of the Tc shift may depend on competition between enhanced electron–phonon coupling and increased electron scattering.
A clear correlation between the magnitude of lattice distortion and Tc is expected.
Phase separation or ordering could independently affect superconductivity.
Failure of increased atomic-size mismatch to produce a statistically significant distortion-correlated Tc shift would falsify the proposed primary-control hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions and boundary require measurements below or well below Tc, whereas determining Tc from resistivity-versus-temperature and magnetic-susceptibility transitions requires measurements spanning the superconducting transition, including temperatures at and above Tc.
